source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: Key Inflection Times of the Day That Set Up Breakouts and Reversals

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; sides field states mirrored/same

candidates.name: KeyInflectionTimeWindow
candidates.quote: The market often breaks out or reverses within a bar before or after 7:00 a.m. and 7:30 a.m. PST on economic reports, at 11:30 a.m. PST, and less often around 11 a.m. and noon PST.
candidates.description: Shared primitive: flag bars within one bar of a short list of specific clock times (7:00, 7:30, 11:00, 11:30, 12:00 PST) as elevated-probability breakout/reversal times, for other entries to gate on.
candidates.pseudocode: isKeyTime = false; for each t in keyTimes: isKeyTime = isKeyTime || (abs(ctx.Time() - t) <= windowBars * barMinutes)

complexity.reason: a fixed set of Time comparisons, no window loop over price

notes: Distinct from the existing TimeWindow rule: that tests an inclusive continuous range; this tests proximity to a small set of discrete instants.

candidates.name: LateMorningStopRunFade
candidates.quote: Very commonly on strong trend days there will be a strong countertrend panic move that will scare people out of their positions, and this normally happens between 11:00 and 11:30 a.m. ... the trend will usually have gone a long way back toward its old extreme.
candidates.description: On an established trend day, near the 11:00-11:30 PST window, a sharp countertrend panic spike that reverses is a fade entry back in the trend's direction.
candidates.pseudocode: R15-01 (11:00-11:30 window) && strongTrendEstablished() && counterTrendSpike(spikeBars) && close[0] crosses back through spike's midpoint -> enter with the trend
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry beyond the reversal bar back in the trend's direction

complexity.reason: combines a time window with trend-strength and spike/climax detection, none of which is a fixed-window calculation

candidates.name: NextDayOppositeDirectionAfterStopRun
candidates.quote: The stop-run pullback usually breaks a significant trend line, so the run to the new extreme (a higher high or lower low test following a trend line break) prompts smart traders to look for a trade in the opposite direction in the first hour of the next day.
candidates.description: After a late-session stop-run breaks a significant trend line and runs to a new extreme, favor a countertrend entry in the first hour of the following session.

complexity.reason: needs trend-line break detection plus state that persists across a session boundary; the exact 'first hour' cutoff is a design decision

candidates.name: TradingRangeDayLateBoundaryTrap
candidates.quote: This type of trap is common on trading range days as well, where the market has been hovering near one extreme for a couple of hours in what appears to be an incipient breakout, only to make a sharp move to take out the other extreme, and this opposite breakout often fails around 11:30 a.m. PST.
candidates.description: On a trading-range day, a breakout through the opposite extreme of the day's range near the 11:30 window that fails traps traders on both sides; favor a fade back into the range afterward.
candidates.pseudocode: isTradingRangeDay() && R15-01 (11:30 window) && breaksOppositeExtremeOfDayRange() && failsToHold() -> fade back into the range
candidates.book_order_type: stop entry back into the range once the opposite-extreme breakout fails

complexity.reason: 'trading range day' has no agreed mechanical definition (per the complexity grade guidance); the rest of the test is otherwise concrete

candidates.name: TradingRangeDayCloseNearMiddleTarget
candidates.quote: Most trading range days close somewhere in the middle.
candidates.description: On a trading-range day, expect/target the session close near the middle of the day's range rather than at either extreme; use this as a profit-taking guide for range-boundary trades taken late in the day.

complexity.reason: depends on the same undefined 'trading range day' classification as R15-04

rejected.quote: Institutions benefit from the sharp countertrend spike because it allows them to add on at much better prices, expecting the trend to resume into the close.
rejected.reason: attributes the move to institutional motive, which is not data the engine has; the tradable residue (the time-window fade) is captured in R15-02

rejected.quote: What causes the move? Institutions ... looking to create or contribute to any rumor that could cause a brief panic that ran stops
rejected.reason: news/rumor causation is data the engine cannot have

chapter_summary: Identifies clock times (7:00, 7:30, 11:00, 11:30, noon PST) when breakouts and reversals cluster, and describes two recurring late-morning traps: a countertrend stop-run panic on trend days that fails and resumes the trend, and a false breakout of the opposite extreme on trading-range days that fails and reverts toward the middle. Produces one simple, reusable time-window primitive (R15-01, distinct from the existing TimeWindow rule's inclusive-range form) and four higher-complexity entries/targets that layer trend-strength, trend-line-break, cross-session, and 'trading range day' concepts on top of it -- all flagged intraday-only. The causal (institutional/news) explanations for the moves are explicitly non-mechanical and rejected.
